knowledge:
- key_parameters: quantCols=Numeric indices or character names of columns containing quantitative intensity data in the input table ;; runCol=Character name of the column containing run identifiers, used to split multi-set data into separate assays ;; name=Character string to name the newly created assay (e.g., "psms", "peptides") ;; fnames=Character string specifying the column to use as row names for the imported assay ;; colData=A DataFrame containing sample annotations; must contain a quantCols column (and runCol for multi-set data) to match annotations ;; removeEmptyCols=Logical; if TRUE, automatically detects and removes columns containing only NA values ;; verbose=Logical; if FALSE, disables console progress messages during data loading ;; i=Name or index of the assay to be processed (e.g., in logTransform, normalize, aggregateFeatures) ;; fcol=Feature variable in the rowData of the source assay used to group features for aggregation (e.g., "Proteins") ;; fun=Function used to aggregate quantitative values (e.g., colMeans or robustSummary) ;; pNA=Numeric value between 0 and 1 specifying the maximum allowed proportion of missing values per row when filtering
- alternatives: readSCPfromDIANN()=Specifically designed to import label-free and plexDIA/mTRAQ Report.tsv files generated by DIA-NN ;; MsDataHub::MsDataHub()=Recommended replacement for the deprecated msdata::quant() function to retrieve benchmark datasets ;; ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap()=Recommended for advanced matrix visualization and heatmap generation with row/column annotations instead of base R plotting
- when_to_use: Use this workflow when processing raw quantitative tables (e.g., from MaxQuant, Proteome Discoverer, Sage, or FragPipe) at the PSM, peptide, or protein level. It is ideal for cleaning, transforming, normalizing, and aggregating mass spectrometry-based proteomics or metabolomics data while maintaining hierarchical links between different levels of features.
- pitfalls: MaxQuant represents missing values as 0 instead of NA. Users must run zeroIsNA() before performing missing value analysis or filtering, otherwise zeros will skew calculations ;; Filtering features using variables that are not present in all assays (e.g., qValue which is only in PSMs) will result in empty assays for the other levels unless the keep argument is configured or filtering is targeted ;; ggplot2 and other tidyverse tools expect standard data.frame or tibble objects, whereas QFeatures uses matrices and DataFrame objects. Users must convert them using as.data.frame() or data.frame(longForm(...)) to avoid plotting errors

workflows.name: quantitative_proteomics_processing
workflows.intent: Import, clean, transform, normalize, and aggregate quantitative mass spectrometry proteomics data from peptide/PSM level to protein level.
input: cptac_a_b_peptides.txt (tabular peptide-level quantification file from MaxQuant or similar software)
workflows.stages:
1. Import tabular data into a QFeatures object using readQFeatures()
2. Encode experimental design in colData()
3. Filter out contaminants and reverse hits using filterFeatures()
4. Select relevant feature variables using selectRowData()
5. Replace zero values with NA using zeroIsNA() and filter missing values using filterNA()
6. Count unique features per sample using countUniqueFeatures()
7. Log-transform quantitative data using logTransform()
8. Normalize data using normalize()
9. Aggregate peptide-level features to protein-level features using aggregateFeatures()
10. Convert to long format for visualization using longForm()
workflows.code:
library("QFeatures")
# Single-set import
hl <- readQFeatures(hlpsms, quantCols = 1:10, name = "psms")

# Multi-set import
hlpsms$FileName <- rep( rep(paste0("run", 1:3, ".raw"), each = 4), length.out = nrow(hlpsms) )
qfMulti <- readQFeatures(hlpsms, quantCols = quantCols, runCol = "FileName")

# Import with colData
coldata <- DataFrame( quantCols = quantCols, condition = rep(c("A", "B"), 5), batch = rep(c("batch1", "batch2"), each = 5) )
qfSingle <- readQFeatures(hlpsms, colData = coldata)

# Processing workflow
cptac <- readQFeatures(x, quantCols = i, name = "peptides", fnames = "Sequence")

# Encoding experimental design
cptac$group <- rep(c("6A", "6B"), each = 3)
cptac$sample <- rep(7:9, 2)

# Filtering out contaminants and reverse hits
cptac <- cptac |> filterFeatures(~ Reverse == "") |> filterFeatures(~ Potential.contaminant == "")

# Removing unneeded feature variables
rowvars <- c("Sequence", "Proteins", "Leading.razor.protein")
cptac <- selectRowData(cptac, rowvars)

# Managing missing values
cptac <- zeroIsNA(cptac, i = seq_along(cptac))
cptac <- filterNA(cptac, i = seq_along(cptac), pNA = 0)

# Counting unique features
cptac <- countUniqueFeatures(cptac, i = "peptides", colDataName = "peptide_counts")
cptac <- countUniqueFeatures(cptac, i = "peptides", groupBy = "Proteins", colDataName = "protein_counts")

# Log transformation
cptac <- logTransform(cptac, i = "peptides", name = "peptides_log")

# Normalisation
cptac <- normalize(cptac, i = "peptides_log", name = "peptides_norm", method = "diff.median")

# Feature aggregation
cptac <- aggregateFeatures(cptac, i = "peptides_norm", fcol = "Proteins", name = "proteins")

# Subsetting and converting to long form
stat3 <- hl["P42227-2", , ]
stat3_df <- data.frame(longForm(stat3))
